questions.q: Define 'popular notion' in the context of psychology and give one example from the textbook.
questions.a: A popular notion is a common-sense explanation of human behaviour based on cultural sayings, hindsight, or anecdotal evidence, not systematic empirical study. Example: "Out of sight, out of mind" or "Distance makes the heart grow fonder." A wrong answer reveals the student may confuse popular notions with scientific theories or think they are the same as hypotheses.

questions.q: Explain why common-sense explanations are considered 'hindsight bias' using the two proverbs about distance and attraction.
questions.a: Common-sense explanations are hindsight bias because they are used after the behaviour occurs to justify it. If you find a new friend, you say "out of sight, out of mind"; if you don't, you say "distance makes the heart grow fonder." The explanation changes to fit the outcome, so it cannot predict behaviour. A wrong answer reveals the student may think both proverbs are scientific hypotheses or that hindsight bias means looking back at history.

questions.q: A teacher believes that giving students only easy problems will build their confidence so they can later solve hard problems. Design a simple experiment based on Dweck (1975) to test this belief.
questions.a: Two groups: Group A gets only easy problems for 25 days; Group B gets mix of easy and hard problems with encouragement to attribute failure to effort. Then give both a new set of hard problems. Measure persistence. Scientific psychology predicts Group B will persist longer. A wrong answer reveals the student may not include a control group, or may not manipulate the independent variable (type of problems), or may not measure the dependent variable (persistence).

questions.q: Compare and contrast the goals of popular notions and scientific psychology in terms of prediction, explanation, and control of behaviour.
questions.a: Popular notions aim to explain behaviour after it occurs (post-hoc), lack predictive power, and cannot control behaviour. Scientific psychology seeks to predict behaviour before it occurs, explain through testable theories, and control behaviour through evidence-based interventions. A wrong answer reveals the student may think popular notions can predict, or that scientific psychology only explains.

questions.q: Critique the statement: 'Scientific psychology is just common sense made complicated.' Use evidence from the Dweck study.
questions.a: The statement is false. Common sense would suggest easy problems build confidence; Dweck's study showed the opposite—students with only easy problems gave up faster when faced with failure. Scientific psychology often contradicts common sense because it tests assumptions empirically. A wrong answer reveals the student may agree with the statement or not use the Dweck study as evidence.

questions.q: Create a new scenario (not from the textbook) where a popular notion and a scientific psychological prediction would differ. Describe both and explain how you would test them.
questions.a: Example: Popular notion: "Opposites attract in relationships." Scientific prediction: "Similarity in attitudes predicts attraction." Test: Survey couples on attitude similarity and relationship satisfaction. A good answer includes a clear popular notion, a testable scientific hypothesis, and a basic experimental design. A poor answer reveals the student may not differentiate between a notion and a hypothesis, or may not propose a feasible test.
